title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 25
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: The Role of Fire in Ecosystems
passages.text:
Fire is one of the most powerful ecological forces shaping terrestrial ecosystems worldwide. Although fire is often perceived as purely destructive, modern ecology recognises that many ecosystems have evolved under fire regimes spanning thousands of years, and that certain plant and animal communities depend on periodic burning for survival and reproduction. Understanding the ecological role of fire is essential for effective land management and conservation, particularly as climate change alters fire frequencies and intensities across the globe.

Fire effects on vegetation vary dramatically depending on fire intensity, season, and ecosystem type. In temperate grasslands and savannas, low-to-moderate intensity fires remove accumulated dead plant material, or "litter," that would otherwise inhibit new growth. This clearing of dead biomass allows fresh herbaceous plants to sprout, providing nutritious forage for grazing animals. In boreal forests of northern latitudes, fire stimulates seed release in fire-adapted conifers such as lodgepole pine and jack pine, which hold seeds in tightly sealed cones. Heat from fire opens these cones, releasing seeds onto prepared seedbeds of ash-enriched soil. Without periodic fire, these forests accumulate excessive dead wood and become choked with dense understory vegetation, reducing habitat quality for wildlife.

Fire also redistributes nutrients through ecosystems in ways that benefit plant growth. The ash from burned vegetation contains potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen — essential macronutrients for plant development. In many forest ecosystems, fire-released nutrients wash into soils during the first post-fire rains, creating a flush of available nutrients that can stimulate vegetation recovery and regeneration. However, the intensity and timing of fires influence this nutrient cycling. Severely hot fires may volatilise nitrogen compounds, causing nutrient loss, whereas cool fires and surface burns preserve more soil nutrient content. Soil structure can also be altered by fire: in hydrophobic soils (water-repellent soils created by intense heat), water infiltration is reduced, which can increase erosion and runoff in the short term.

Many plant species have evolved fire-adapted traits enabling them to survive or even require fire for reproduction. Serotinous cones — cones that only release seeds after exposure to heat — are found in pines, firs, and eucalypts across fire-prone regions. Some shrub species, including manzanita in California chaparral, have hard seed coats that germinate only after being scarified by fire heat, a mechanism that synchronises seedling emergence with the post-fire nutrient-rich environment. Other species recover from fire through vigorous sprouting from basal meristems (growth tissue at the base of the plant) and extensive root systems that survive fire beneath the soil surface. These adaptations demonstrate that fire is not an aberration in these ecosystems but an integral part of their evolutionary history.

Fire also shapes animal communities and behaviour. Many insects, including bark beetles that feed on dead wood, depend on recently burned forests. Large herbivores such as elk and moose benefit from the flush of palatable vegetation that emerges in the years following fire. Conversely, some cavity-nesting birds rely on dead trees (snags) created by non-lethal fires, which provide shelter and nesting sites for decades. In fire-suppressed ecosystems where natural burning has been prevented for decades, wildlife populations often decline because essential habitat features disappear. The decline of spotted owls in Pacific Northwest forests has been partly attributed to fire suppression, which allowed forests to become too dense and old-growth, lacking the structural diversity that owls require.

Human fire suppression in the twentieth century fundamentally altered fire-adapted ecosystems. The policy of total fire exclusion, epitomised by Smokey Bear's "Only you can prevent forest fires" campaign beginning in 1944, created landscapes with excessive fuel accumulation and altered plant composition. Decades of fire suppression in western North America, Australia, and Mediterranean regions have left forests vulnerable to catastrophic megafires — uncontrolled wildfires of unprecedented scale — when conditions finally ignite. Modern land management has begun reversing this legacy through controlled burns (also called prescribed burns), deliberately lit, carefully monitored fires that reduce dangerous fuel loads while promoting ecosystem health. These prescribed burns mimic the natural fire regimes that shaped ecosystems before industrial fire suppression, restoring ecological balance and reducing the risk of catastrophic wildfires.

passages.title: Language Extinction and Preservation
passages.text:
Language extinction represents a catastrophic loss of human cultural and linguistic diversity. Linguists estimate that one language disappears roughly every two weeks, and that of the approximately 7,000 languages currently spoken worldwide, nearly half will be extinct by the end of the twenty-first century if current trends continue. This rate of extinction is unprecedented in human history and mirrors the collapse of biodiversity in natural ecosystems, earning it the term "linguistic extinction." Each lost language erases centuries of cultural knowledge, unique ways of categorising and understanding the world, and irreplaceable oral traditions.

Language death occurs through a process called language shift, where younger generations cease speaking their heritage language in favour of a dominant, often national or international language. This typically happens when a language becomes associated with economic disadvantage or social stigma, while speakers of the dominant language enjoy better opportunities in education, employment, and social mobility. In many regions, globalisation and urbanisation have accelerated language shift. For example, in parts of India, indigenous languages like Gondi (spoken by approximately 2.7 million people) face pressure from Hindi and English. Similarly, in the Pacific region, many languages spoken by fewer than 10,000 speakers have been largely abandoned by young people who prefer English or regional lingua francas.

Critical mass — the minimum number of speakers needed to sustain a language across generations — typically requires at least several thousand native speakers. Languages with fewer than 1,000 speakers face particularly acute risks, as they lack sufficient numbers of intergenerational transmission. Many endangered languages exist in what linguists call a "grandmother-grandchild gap": elderly speakers retain fluency, but middle-aged adults have limited proficiency, and children have minimal exposure. When the eldest generation passes away and no younger speakers have achieved full proficiency, the language effectively dies within that community.

Language preservation efforts take multiple forms, each with distinct strengths and limitations. Community-based revitalisation programmes, such as immersion schools in New Zealand where Maori is the primary language of instruction, have successfully halted language decline and increased the number of fluent young speakers. The Maori-language revival, beginning in the 1980s with the establishment of kōhanga reo (language nests — early-childhood immersion centres), has transformed Maori from a near-extinct language to one with several hundred thousand speakers across the country. Digital archiving initiatives, such as the Endangered Languages Archive (ELAN) and the Linguistic Atlas of India, preserve spoken recordings, transcriptions, and grammatical documentation of vulnerable languages. These archives serve as historical records and can support community revitalisation even if primary speakers eventually pass away.

The value of language preservation extends beyond cultural preservation. Indigenous languages often encode sophisticated ecological and botanical knowledge accumulated over centuries. Australian Aboriginal languages, for instance, contain detailed taxonomies of plants and animals and sophisticated understandings of seasonal patterns and land management practices. When a language disappears, this embodied knowledge is frequently lost. Additionally, languages demonstrate remarkable cognitive diversity in how they structure meaning. Some languages lack a strict past-future tense distinction, others employ ergative grammar (where the subject of an intransitive verb is marked like the object of a transitive verb), and still others possess elaborate systems for marking evidentiality — whether information comes from direct experience, hearsay, or inference. These linguistic structures reveal human cognitive flexibility and contribute to our understanding of language universals and variation.

Language preservation requires sustained community commitment, institutional support, and often government policy recognising indigenous language rights. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) affirms the right of indigenous peoples to use, maintain, and revitalise their languages. Countries including New Zealand, Australia, Canada, and Mexico have implemented policy frameworks supporting indigenous language education and documentation. However, preservation efforts face significant challenges: limited funding, competing economic pressures, and the powerful cultural cachet of globally dominant languages. Success stories like the Maori revival demonstrate that language extinction is not inevitable, but rather depends on deliberate, sustained intervention and the willing participation of language communities themselves.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what effect does low-to-moderate intensity fire have on grasslands and savannas?
questions.correctAnswer: It removes dead plant material and allows new herbaceous plants to grow
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that in grasslands and savannas, such fires 'remove accumulated dead plant material' that 'inhibits new growth,' allowing 'fresh herbaceous plants to sprout.'
options: It destroys all vegetation permanently
It removes dead plant material and allows new herbaceous plants to grow
It increases the accumulation of dead wood
It prevents nutrient cycling in soils

questions.prompt: The word 'stimulates' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: triggers or promotes
questions.explanation: 'Stimulates' means to trigger or cause something to happen, as in how fire stimulates seed release.
options: triggers or promotes
prevents or blocks
slowly develops
temporarily pauses

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, which nutrients are released into soils when vegetation burns?
questions.correctAnswer: Potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explicitly states that ash contains 'potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen — essential macronutrients for plant development.'
options: Calcium, magnesium, and sulphur
Potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen
Iron, zinc, and copper
Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about serotinous cones?
questions.correctAnswer: They are an adaptation that links seed release to fire occurrence
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that serotinous cones 'only release seeds after exposure to heat,' indicating this is an evolved mechanism connecting seed dispersal to fire events.
options: They are found only in tropical rainforests
They are an adaptation that links seed release to fire occurrence
They prevent seed germination in all conditions
They evolved as a recent response to climate change

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the decline of spotted owls in paragraph 5?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate how fire suppression negatively affects wildlife habitat and populations
questions.explanation: The spotted owl example demonstrates that fire suppression reduces structural forest diversity, which harms wildlife dependent on specific habitat features.
options: To argue that owls should be considered invasive species
To illustrate how fire suppression negatively affects wildlife habitat and populations
To show that all cavity-nesting birds are extinct
To explain why fire should be completely prevented

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 6, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a consequence of twentieth-century fire suppression?
questions.correctAnswer: Increased agricultural productivity
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6 discusses fuel accumulation, altered plant composition, and catastrophic megafires — but not agricultural productivity.
options: Excessive fuel accumulation in forests
Altered plant composition in ecosystems
Increased vulnerability to catastrophic megafires
Increased agricultural productivity

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is the modern ecological view of fire?
questions.correctAnswer: Many ecosystems have evolved under fire regimes and depend on periodic burning
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that 'many ecosystems have evolved under fire regimes spanning thousands of years, and that certain plant and animal communities depend on periodic burning for survival.'
options: Fire is entirely destructive and should always be prevented
Fire has no ecological value
Many ecosystems have evolved under fire regimes and depend on periodic burning
Fire only affects a few rare species

questions.prompt: The word 'volatilise' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: convert to vapor or gas
questions.explanation: 'Volatilise' means to convert a substance into vapor or gas form, as in how intense heat can volatilise nitrogen.
options: convert to vapor or gas
dissolve in water
absorb into soil
break into small pieces

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'In hydrophobic soils (water-repellent soils created by intense heat), water infiltration is reduced, which can increase erosion and runoff in the short term.'
questions.correctAnswer: Intense fire creates water-repellent soil that increases erosion and runoff
questions.explanation: The sentence explains a cause-effect relationship: hydrophobic soils reduce water absorption, leading to increased erosion.
options: All soils are hydrophobic after fire
Water infiltration always improves after fire
Intense fire creates water-repellent soil that increases erosion and runoff
Erosion and runoff prevent fires from spreading

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes fire's ecological role (A), plant adaptations to fire (C), and how suppression has caused ecological problems (E).
options: A. Fire is an integral part of many terrestrial ecosystems and has shaped plant and animal communities over millennia.
B. All fires are beneficial and should be encouraged regardless of intensity or context.
C. Many plant species have evolved fire-adapted traits including serotinous cones and basal sprouting.
D. Prescribed burns should never be used as they are always dangerous.
E. Twentieth-century fire suppression policies have created dangerous fuel accumulations and altered ecosystem composition.
F. Fire only affects pine trees and not other plant species.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, approximately how many languages currently exist worldwide?
questions.correctAnswer: Approximately 7,000 languages
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states 'of the approximately 7,000 languages currently spoken worldwide, nearly half will be extinct by the end of the twenty-first century.'
options: Approximately 1,000 languages
Approximately 3,500 languages
Approximately 7,000 languages
Approximately 15,000 languages

questions.prompt: The word 'linguistic' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: related to language
questions.explanation: 'Linguistic' is an adjective referring to language or languages, as in 'linguistic diversity' and 'linguistic extinction.'
options: related to language
related to music
related to mathematics
related to biology

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what is language shift?
questions.correctAnswer: The process where younger generations stop speaking their heritage language in favor of a dominant language
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines language shift as 'where younger generations cease speaking their heritage language in favour of a dominant, often national or international language.'
options: The creation of new languages through linguistic evolution
The process where younger generations stop speaking their heritage language in favor of a dominant language
The gradual expansion of a minority language
The formal study of historical languages

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss the Maori language revival in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To demonstrate a successful language revitalisation programme using immersion education
questions.explanation: The Maori example illustrates how kōhanga reo immersion centres successfully halted decline and increased fluent speakers.
options: To show that all endangered languages are now extinct
To demonstrate a successful language revitalisation programme using immersion education
To argue that language preservation is impossible
To explain why English should replace all other languages

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the critical mass of speakers?
questions.correctAnswer: Languages with fewer than 1,000 speakers face severe risk of extinction
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states 'Languages with fewer than 1,000 speakers face particularly acute risks, as they lack sufficient numbers of intergenerational transmission.'
options: All languages with fewer than 10,000 speakers are already extinct
Critical mass is never necessary for language survival
Languages with fewer than 1,000 speakers face severe risk of extinction
Large speaker populations guarantee language preservation

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, what type of knowledge do indigenous languages often encode?
questions.correctAnswer: Ecological and botanical knowledge accumulated over centuries
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states 'Indigenous languages often encode sophisticated ecological and botanical knowledge accumulated over centuries.'
options: Only modern scientific terminology
Ecological and botanical knowledge accumulated over centuries
Abstract mathematical concepts only
Religious dogma without practical value

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, which is NOT mentioned as a feature of linguistic diversity?
questions.correctAnswer: Universal sameness in all language structures
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 emphasizes cognitive diversity and variation in language structures — not sameness.
options: Diverse tense systems across languages
Ergative grammar in some languages
Evidentiality marking systems
Universal sameness in all language structures

questions.prompt: The word 'embodied' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: incorporated or expressed in
questions.explanation: 'Embodied knowledge' refers to knowledge that is incorporated within or expressed through languages and cultural practices.
options: physically located in bodies
incorporated or expressed in
forgotten or lost entirely
scientifically proven

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) affirms the right of indigenous peoples to use, maintain, and revitalise their languages.'
questions.correctAnswer: International law recognizes indigenous peoples' rights to preserve and use their languages
questions.explanation: The sentence conveys that international policy supports indigenous language maintenance and revitalization.
options: The United Nations forbids indigenous languages
International law recognizes indigenous peoples' rights to preserve and use their languages
Indigenous language rights are not protected by any laws
All indigenous languages must be replaced with English

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: B,D,F
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes language extinction rates and causes (B), the value of indigenous knowledge (D), and that preservation requires deliberate intervention (F).
options: A. All indigenous languages are already completely extinct.
B. Language extinction occurs through language shift when dominant languages offer economic advantages.
C. Digital archives can never help preserve endangered languages.
D. Indigenous languages encode unique ecological and cognitive knowledge that is lost when languages disappear.
E. Language preservation is impossible and should not be attempted.
F. Successful language revitalization requires community commitment, institutional support, and policy frameworks.
